stories.headline: Delivery completed: On the GST Council meet, reforms
stories.deck: With the latest reforms, GST might finally become a ‘good and simple tax’
stories.bodyText:
The decisions taken by the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council in its 57th meeting on Thursday reveal two distinct changes in the attitude of the tax administration: increased trust in the taxpayer, and reduced anxiety over tax revenues. This is a big change from the system in place so far, where taxpayers have been bogged down by compliance requirements, and the tax enforcement has used this complexity to try to extract every rupee it can. The data show gross collections have not often deviated significantly from the mean over the last two years. After nine years, taxpayers have also become familiar, if not comfortable, with the tax filing system. The previous meeting also rectified most rate-related issues in GST and even reduced the number of slabs, a major driver of the complexity of the tax system. The time was ripe for a significant overhaul of the processes and administration of GST, and the Council has delivered. Thursday’s reforms address complications in the entire chain of GST paperwork, from registration and return filing, to refunds and litigation. The thrust is to reduce human discretion in these processes by automating registrations, reducing the number of times small businesses have to file returns, handling refunds through computer-based verification, and significantly reducing the powers of GST officers. In essence, trust the taxpayer to comply, and crack down only when non-compliance is demonstrable. That is the way it should be, instead of a ‘guilty until proven innocent’ approach.
While all the simplification measures are welcome, some specific ones deserve special mention as they will substantially ease areas of major discontent. So far, taxpayers were denied input tax credits (ITC) until their suppliers had filed their returns. This meant that thousands of genuine businesses that had received supplies and paid taxes on them were denied ITC, leading to a drying up of crucial working capital. The GST Council has tasked a committee to find a solution that can be implemented by April 1. Removing the arrest powers of GST officers is another step that will significantly reduce harassment, as will tightening the rules around inspection, searches, and seizures of consignments. The Centre has also used this opportunity to introduce a faceless assessment system for Central GST registered companies, along the lines of the popular faceless system in income tax. The decision to review rates only once a year, and implement rate changes only at the start of financial years, removes significant uncertainty that usually arises each time the Council meets. In its 10th year, GST is finally starting to look like what it should have at the time of rollout.

briefs.headline: Now, RBI puts CRR and bond sale into play
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: RBI has tightened daily cash reserve requirements for banks, impounding an additional Rs 1 lakh crore, and has announced a Rs 25,000 crore bond sale, moves that will drain liquidity from the banking system and put upward pressure on overnight money market rates amid pressure on prices as well as the exchange rate from the intensifying conflict in West Asia.
The liquidity-draining measure will hasten the transmission of the 25-basis-point repo rate cut announced by the central bank on Oct 7.
RBI has raised the minimum daily cash reserve ratio (CRR) requirement from 90% to 99% of the prescribed level, effective from the fortnight beginning Oct 16, 2026. The open market operation (OMO) sale auction of govt of India securities worth Rs 25,000 crore is on Oct 13. Using aggregate deposits of around Rs 284 lakh crore as a rough proxy, the maximum additional daily CRR balance works out to approximately Rs 1 lakh crore (with daily CRR increasing from 3.6% to 3.96% of deposits).
Banks are required to maintain a CRR of 4% of their deposits. The statutory ratio remains unchanged, but RBI has reduced the flexibility banks have in meeting the requirement during the fortnight. Previously, banks could maintain at least 90% of the prescribed CRR on each day, provided their average daily balance over the reporting fortnight met the full requirement.
Under the revised norms, banks must maintain at least 99% of the prescribed CRR every day while continuing to meet the full requirement on average over the fortnight.
This will require banks to keep a larger portion of their deposits with RBI on a daily basis, reducing the funds available to meet short-term liquidity needs. Dealers said that since banks cannot predict the extent of deposits accurately, they need to err on the side of caution to avoid defaulting on CRR and end up maintaining more than the statutory requirement.

briefs.headline: Bank credit up 20% year-on-year in end September
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Banks concluded the first half of FY27 with an acceleration in balance-sheet expansion, as year-on-year credit growth climbed to 19.4% and aggregate deposit growth reached 17.8%, leaving the credit-to-deposit ratio at 81%.
Total bank credit stood at over Rs 229.9 lakh crore as of Sept 30, while aggregate deposits reached about Rs 284 lakh crore. Many large banks that have submitted their business figures to the exchanges have attributed the increase to the $133 billion mobilised under the FCNR(B) scheme.
The year-on-year deposit growth at the end of the first quarter (June 30 2026) was 13.3% while the growth in advances was 18.6% A year earlier, at the end of Sept 2025, bank credit growth stood at 11.4%, while aggregate deposits grew 9.9%. Time deposits were the primary driver of deposit accretion, contributing Rs 36.3 lakh crore, or 84.5% of total annual deposit growth, to reach Rs 246.6 lakh crore.
This represented annual growth of 17.3%, compared with 8.8% a year earlier. Demand deposits rose 21.6%, or Rs 6.6 lakh crore, year-on-year to Rs 37.4 lakh crore, up from growth of 18.5% a year earlier.
With credit growth outstripping deposit growth, banks are facing tighter resource constraints, with the credit-to-deposit ratio remaining above 80%. During the fortnight ended Sept 30, 2026, credit expansion lifted the credit-to-deposit ratio to 81%. From 78.9% at the end of Sept 2024, the ratio rose to 80.8% in March 2025. By Sept 30, 2025, deposit inflows had brought it down to 79.9%. Lending accelerated in the second half of FY26, and the ratio reached an interim peak of 81.4% on March 31, 2026.

briefs.headline: PERM freeze: Indian IT stocks rally, but talent exodus looms
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU/HUDERABAD: Even as the US govt suspended processing under the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme for some Indian IT firms, potentially jeopardising eligible employees’ pathways to permanent residency, the sector’s stocks rallied on Friday, suggesting limited market concern amid declining dependence on H-1B visas.
However, the suspension could create talent retention and hiring challenges. H-1B employees may move to employers not covered by the suspension to keep their green card applications on track, potentially triggering an exodus of skilled professionals. Top talent may also hesitate to join affected companies if doing so means losing a viable pathway to permanent residency.
Vikram Shroff, partner for employment, labour and benefits at AZB & Partners, said the suspension should not affect Indian IT companies’ ability to service US clients, although it could delay new applications. “It is hoped that the suspension is temporary and is withdrawn once the investigation is completed,” he said.
TCS said the PERM programme suspension was unlikely to affect its workforce strategy or customer engagements, as its applications under the programme had been in single digits over the past two years.
“Our original business model has always been that people go from here, work on the project, go onsite, spend two, three years there, and come back. 
So there is a continuous movement of talent between onsite and offshore,” TCS CEO K Krithivasan said.
As of October last year, TCS had around 11,000 H-1B employees in its 32,000-33,000-strong US workforce. While acknowledging that some employees may want to stay in the US permanently, Krithivasan said permanent residency had never been central to the company’s workforce strategy. Local employees account for 50% of TCS’s US workforce, and the company plans to hire another 15,000 people there over five years.
Microsoft said 80% of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees. Applications for new hires accounted for just 1% of its US workforce and involved individuals already legally present in the country.
“We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work,” the company said in a statement.
Cyrus D Mehta, managing partner of New York-based law firm Cyrus D Mehta & Partners, called the suspension a “warped approach”. “Immigration is not a zero-sum game,” he said, disputing the suggestion that hiring foreign workers necessarily takes jobs away from Americans. Responding to Vice-President 
JD Vance
’s criticism of Microsoft over its 2025 layoffs, Mehta said the layoffs did not prevent companies from recruiting foreign workers with specialised skills.
Stephen Yale-Loehr, a retired professor of immigration law practice at Cornell Law School, called the Department of Labor’s action illegal, arguing that companies had not been given a due process hearing before their applications were suspended.
“I am sure the companies will sue. But litigation takes time, and in the meantime these companies can’t use the PERM green card system. This is another attack on legal immigration by the Trump administration,” he said.
David J Bier, director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute, said he viewed the current US administration as the most hostile to legal immigration of any administration.
Industry leaders said the suspension affecting eight major technology companies could accelerate the shift of high-value technology work to India and boost growth in global capability centres (GCCs), despite a limited immediate impact.
Former HCL Technologies CEO Vineet Nayar said Indian IT companies accounted for fewer than 1,400 of the 117,849 PERM certifications issued last year, suggesting the direct impact could be limited. He said the move could accelerate the relocation of US technology work to India.
Former Tech Mahindra CEO CP Gurnani and co-founder and vice-chairman of AIONOS, said India should use the opportunity to attract experienced technology talent back home.
Nasscom senior vice-president and chief strategy officer Sangeeta Gupta said the business impact was likely to be negligible, as companies had filed few PERM applications in recent years and the move was prospective, not retrospective.

briefs.headline: Ownership issues cloud TVS’ Venu Srinivasan, family
briefs.deck: Sudarshan Venu, the 37-year-old CMD of TVS Motor Company, named as Significant Beneficial Owner (SBO) sets cats among pigeons
briefs.bodyText:
Significant differences have emerged over the interpretation of ownership and succession plans within the family of Venu Srinivasan, involving his wife, Mallika Srinivasan, daughter Lakshmi Venu and son Sudarshan Venu, in relation to their interests in TVS Motor Company and its holding firm, TVS Holdings Limited. They are the third and fourth generation members of the TVS Group founder T.V. Sundaram Iyengar’s family.
The differences came into focus in April 2025, The Hindu has reliably learned, when TVS Holdings disclosed that Sudarshan Venu, the 37-year-old chairman and managing director of TVS Motor Company was named as a Significant Beneficial Owner (SBO). The company’s shareholding disclosure records April 16, 2025, as the date of acquisition of his significant beneficial interest through the VS Trust, in which his father, Venu Srinivasan, is a trustee, and the Srinivasan Trust.
The disclosure has drawn attention to the succession of ownership of TVS Motor, the flagship business within the TVS Group, valued at over ₹1.80 lakh crore.
The disagreement centres on the interpretation of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) among the four family members, dated March 20, 2024, and executed on March 21. Its salient features were disclosed to the stock exchanges on March 22. The MoU sets out non-compete obligations and restrictions on the use of the TVS brand and trademarks in specified businesses. TVS Holdings clarified that it was not a party to the agreement.
Under the disclosed terms, Mr. Sudarshan and persons controlled by him agreed not to use certain trademarks, including TVS, in specified die-casting businesses, and not to compete for a defined period in agricultural machinery, including tractors and self-propelled farm equipment. Ms. Mallika and Ms. Lakshmi, in turn, agreed not to use certain trademarks in businesses including two- and three-wheelers, financial services and real estate, and not to compete in specified vehicle-related businesses.
An executive with direct knowledge of the ongoing dispute said the MoU did not discuss ownership transition. “Does any CEO or MD automatically, become the owner as well? When we look across India, or globally, it’s stating the obvious - the distinction between distributed ownership and management,” the executive said. The executive said attempts to seek clarity on the April 2025 SBO disclosure had been met with “silence”.
Ms. Lakshmi is understood to have the support of her mother, Ms. Mallika, in seeking an amicable resolution. “She wishes to sit across and settle differences,” the executive said, adding that Ms. Lakshmi sought an equal share of the business, as the division reflected in the disclosures and the MoU was considered “very unfair”.
The dispute has also brought allegations of gender bias into focus. An executive said Ms. Mallika and Mr. Venu had raised their children to believe in equality as a value, and that the present arrangement was at odds with this principle. “What Ms. Lakshmi is asking for is equality in ownership, and Ms. Mallika supports her on this, but has emphasised on an amicable resolution,” the executive said.
Ms. Lakshmi and Ms. Mallika are also understood to be concerned about the inclusion of the Amalgamations Group in the succession discussions. “Ms. Mallika is herself only a shareholder in that group, so how can she speak for herself without even consulting other shareholding members of the family? She is running TAFE only as a custodian of the firm,” the executive said, describing the inclusion of the Amalgamations Group in the ownership tussle as “mischievous”.
The wider family arrangement provides important context. The Memorandum of Family Arrangement, dated December 10, 2020, covered four branches of the TVS family and sought to align ownership of businesses with the branches managing them and reduce cross-holdings. The arrangement was disclosed to the stock exchanges in December 2020, with further details provided in January 2021. Its implementation involved subsequent corporate restructuring, with February 4, 2022, marking an important date in the process.
The restructuring left Mr. Venu’s branch with control of the group’s flagship automotive interests through TVS Holdings, which was formed out of the restructuring of the erstwhile Sundaram-Clayton. TVS Holdings now holds 50.26% of TVS Motor Company. The separate Sundaram-Clayton entity houses the die-casting business. The ownership structure of these entities is central to the dispute as the family settlement aligned the ownership of businesses with the branches managing them.
The settlement also involved obligations of about ₹2,000 crore payable to other family branches. According to TVS Holdings’ information memorandum, Sundaram-Clayton diluted about 7% of its stake in TVS Motor in FY2022, raising about ₹2,100 crore. The company’s disclosures also describe financing arrangements connected with the settlement obligations. Subsequent reports have attributed the funding and settlement of the dues to Mr. Venu Srinivasan and Mr. Sudarshan Venu.
Lawyers who spoke to The Hindu said an SBO declaration, by itself, should not be construed as a transfer of ownership. Corporate lawyer Karthik Sheshadri, who practises before the Madras High Court, said the primary document underlying the declaration must be examined. “A primary document can be a trust deed, an arrangement, a transfer document, that may not necessarily be disclosed as that is not a requirement, but it has to be the basis for a SBO disclosure,” he said.
“Regulatory filings can be unilateral, which is why it has irked one party. And often, such filings are done at a corporate secretarial level, and they would do it on behalf of the person who controls the company. This is where disputes arise,” Mr. Sheshadri added.

briefs.headline: Teacher denied gratuity for working past 60; Allahabad HC orders payment with 6% interest
briefs.deck: A woman joined an educational institution in Faizabad as an assistant teacher on August 16, 1992. She continued working there until March 31, 2019, when she retired. However, the institution declined to pay her gratuity, arguing that the prescribed retirement age was 60 and she had remained in service until she was 62.
briefs.bodyText:
You work several years in an educational institution and are denied 
gratuity
 on the grounds that you worked beyond the retirement age. What do you do? In one such case a retired teacher was denied gratuity and she challenged it in court.
What the case is about
A woman joined an educational institution in Faizabad as an assistant teacher on August 16, 1992. She continued working there until March 31, 2019, when she retired. However, the institution declined to pay her gratuity, arguing that the prescribed retirement age was 60 and she had remained in service until she was 62.
On September 13, 2023, the Principal Secretary of the Uttar Pradesh Government's Minority Welfare Department rejected her claim for gratuity. The decision was based solely on the fact that she had continued working beyond the age of 60 and retired at 62.
Also Read | 
Sisters sought share in parents’ properties under Hindu Succession law; Madras HC rules for brother over mother’s land on ouster, father’s estate over missing parties
The retired teacher challenged the decision in court, arguing that working beyond the prescribed retirement age should not deprive her of gratuity. She pointed out that she had served the institution continuously for several years before retiring on March 31, 2019.
Her challenge succeeded on September 30, 2026, when the Allahabad High Court directed the educational institution to pay her outstanding gratuity immediately, along with interest at 6% from 2019.
Why did the retired teacher win the gratuity case?
The Allahabad High Court noted that the state-regulated madrasa had refused to pay the woman’s gratuity by relying on government orders and rules, according to an ET report. According to the institution, she had failed to exercise her option to receive gratuity within the stipulated period.
However, the court pointed out that she had been allowed to continue working until the age of 62 and had received all other retirement benefits admissible to her.
The Allahabad High Court observed that merely citing the applicable government orders and alleging that the employee had not exercised the required option was insufficient to settle the question of her gratuity entitlement.
Also Read | 
Retired bank employee got Rs 12.27 lakh leave encashment and claimed Rs 3 lakh exemption in 2020, but government later hiked limit to Rs 25 lakh in 2023; ITAT Chennai allows full tax exemption
This was particularly relevant because the issue of denying gratuity on the basis of such an option had subsequently been examined authoritatively by both the Allahabad High Court and the Supreme Court, the report said.
The court said that once the legal implications of allowing an employee to remain in service beyond the prescribed retirement age had been examined, and it had been held that such an extension could not, in the circumstances considered, justify denial of gratuity, the institution was required to assess the retired teacher’s claim in accordance with that legal position.
The Allahabad High Court also referred to a Supreme Court judgment recognising gratuity as a beneficial scheme intended to protect eligible employees, reinforcing the principle that the benefit should be paid to those entitled to receive it.
The Allahabad High Court observed that the teacher had been permitted to remain in service until March 31, 2019, when she turned 62, and had continued working accordingly. While settling her retirement benefits, the institution could not disregard the legal consequences arising from her extended service.
Also Read | 
US-based daughter files case against parents seeking share in properties; Karnataka HC rejects her ‘ancestral’ claim, saying they were father's separate assets, not coparcenary property
The court further noted that the order rejecting her gratuity claim did not show that the institution had independently examined her entitlement to the benefit. Instead, the rejection rested on the allegation that she had not exercised the option to retire at the age of 60.
Advocate Mayank Parashar of law firm Clasis Law explained to ET that Indian labour laws have traditionally placed employees' social security interests at the centre.
Under both the new Labour Codes and the earlier legal framework, the circumstances in which gratuity can be denied are restricted. Continuing in employment beyond the retirement age with the employer's permission does not, by itself, constitute a valid ground for disqualification.
According to Parashar, the retired woman succeeded because the reason cited for withholding her gratuity was not recognised as a legally valid ground under the applicable law.
Although the judgment concerned an employee of a madrasa operating under state regulation, Parashar said its significance extends to establishments more broadly, including private-sector employers. The ruling underscores the need to assess gratuity claims properly before making a decision.
Employers must have a clear and legally defensible reason before withholding or refusing gratuity or any other social security benefit, he added.
The Allahabad High Court ruled in the retired teacher’s favour, entitling her to receive the outstanding gratuity along with interest at 6%.

briefs.headline: Coal supplies to power plants rise 36% from September lows; rail loading hits 465 rakes a day
briefs.deck: The Coal Ministry stated that rail loading has also improved, stock depletion and power demand are also expected to moderate mid-October citing historical trends.
briefs.bodyText:
Daily coal supplies to the power sector have risen 36% from their post-monsoon lows in September and are averaging about 9% higher in October than in the preceding month, the government said on Friday, signalling an improvement in fuel availability for power generation.
Rail-based supplies have also been strengthened, with an average of 465 rakes dispatched daily in October, the government said, adding that road-based supplies had improved as well.
Last month, state-owned Coal India and its subsidiaries offered power plants with existing supply agreements the option to lift additional coal beyond their annual contracted quantities through road transport, supplementing their regular rail-based supplies.
The Coal Ministry expects daily rail loading of 465–475 rakes to be sufficient to meet power demand, which is expected to moderate by mid-October in line with historical trends.
“With the monsoon receding and peak demand expected to moderate by mid-October (as per historical trends) sustained loading of 465–475 rakes per day should support further stabilisation and enable stock rebuilding ahead of the festive, winter and subsequent summer demand periods, thereby reducing the number of plants in the critical category,” it stated.
The ministry also said the depletion of coal stocks — the difference between consumption and incoming supplies — had slowed sharply, from 0.243 million tonnes (MT) a day in September to 0.116 MT in October.
“The position is therefore stabilising, although stock rebuilding is yet to commence,” it added.
The ministry’s statement came in response to reports flagging concerns over low coal inventories at power plants.
Clarifying the significance of plants classified under the ‘critical stock’ category, it said the criterion — which identifies plants holding less than the prescribed threshold of normative coal stocks — was primarily intended as an early-warning mechanism to flag potential shortages.
“A plant appearing on this list is, by design, an early-warning entry and not an indication that it has run out of coal or is at imminent risk of shutting down,” it argued.

briefs.headline: UPI vs credit cards: What should you choose for payments after MDR?
briefs.deck: The overall value of a transaction depends on several factors including the payment mode, transaction value, the applicable MDR (if any), and the value-back attached to the payment method. This becomes particularly relevant as UPI increasingly intersects with the credit card ecosystem through RuPay credit cards.
briefs.bodyText:
The author is CEO of Paisabazaar
When it comes to choosing between UPI and credit cards, consumers should look at the overall value that they can derive from each payment method rather than the immediate cost of the transaction. While UPI provides convenience and simplicity, credit cards offer cashback, rewards and additional perks. With MDR on higher-value UPI transactions now being discussed, understanding the complete economics of a transaction becomes even more important.
The overall value of a transaction depends on several factors including the payment mode, transaction value, the applicable MDR (if any), and the value-back attached to the payment method. This becomes particularly relevant as UPI increasingly intersects with the credit card ecosystem through RuPay credit cards.
UPI and cards serve different purposes in the consumer wallet
When a consumer makes a UPI payment from a bank account, the money is deducted directly from the account. While this offers simplicity and convenience, such payments generally do not come with any meaningful rewards, apart from occasional merchant-specific offers.
A credit card changes this equation. The consumer can make the purchase today and get an interest-free period of 40-50 days, depending on the card's billing cycle and payment terms. 
Moreover, when it is a RuPay Credit Card that supports UPI payments, this flexibility is combined with the convenience of UPI.
What determines value of a payment?
Value-back as rewards or cashback can change the economics
Credit cards are increasingly being designed around specific spending behaviours. Depending on the card, consumers can earn cashback or reward points on categories ranging from everyday purchases to high-ticket spends like travel bookings and electronics.
Consider a Rs. 50,000 transaction on a card offering 5% cashback on the spend. The consumer could potentially receive Rs 2,500 back, subject to the card's terms, redemption value and applicable caps. Now if the consumer chooses to pay the same amount through UPI and the merchant passes on the entire MDR cost of 0.4% to the consumer, they will end up paying an additional Rs 200, making the product costlier for them, with no additional benefits.
In fact, in most scenarios, credit cards can offer greater value to consumers through rewards, cashback and other benefits, without any additional payment processing charges being levied on them. However, this holds true only if consumers pay their credit card bills in full and on time, avoiding interest or finance charges. Once interest starts accruing on outstanding balances, it can outweigh the value earned through rewards or cashback, potentially nullifying the benefits of using a credit card.
This is why comparing payment methods purely on the basis of transaction charges like MDR could be misleading. Rewards, offers and other value-back systems should also be taken into account. At the same time, a card may carry an annual or joining fee, impose reward caps, exclude certain categories, or offer a lower reward rate on certain transactions – which should also be considered.
Transaction size alone does not determine the better choice
A common assumption is that UPI is best suited to small purchases while cards make more sense for larger transactions. However, in practice, the answer is more nuanced.
Even a small Rs 500 transaction on a credit card could be more valuable than the same transaction through bank-account UPI if the card offers meaningful cashback or rewards on that particular spend. Conversely, a Rs 50,000 transaction may not necessarily justify the use of a credit card if the transaction falls outside the card's reward categories or has already exhausted the applicable monthly reward cap.
Consumers should, therefore, look at the frequency of spending and the cumulative rewards generated over time. Small individual transactions can add up to significant value when they form a large portion of monthly expenditure. At the same time, card-specific discounts, cashback, merchant offers and reward points may add further value. Hence, the effective benefit can vary considerably across cards and merchants, irrespective of transaction values.
Does Transaction Size Decide the  Payment Method?
Credit cards can offer value beyond the immediate transaction
An often-overlooked aspect of credit card payments is that their value is not limited to rewards. For consumers who manage their credit responsibly, the interest-free period can provide useful cash-flow flexibility. Some transactions may also be eligible for EMI conversion, allowing a large purchase to be spread across several months. Credit cards also come with issuer-specific offers, milestone benefits, travel privileges and more.
But these benefits only have value when they are actually relevant to the consumer. Paying an annual fee for benefits that are rarely used does not necessarily make economic sense.
The consumer's spending pattern should drive the choice
Ultimately, there is no single payment method that will offer the best value for every consumer or every transaction. The important shift is to stop looking at payment methods only through the lens of convenience or transaction value and instead consider the net economics of the payment and choose the payment instrument that delivers the most meaningful value for one's individual spending pattern.
Before you tap, scan, or swipe: Check these 6 things
MDR may change the equation, but not necessarily in the same way for everyone
The discussion around MDR on higher-value UPI transactions adds another dimension to this comparison. MDR represents a cost associated with accepting a digital payment, and the relative economics for merchants can vary across payment instruments and transaction types.
The impact on consumers, however, will depend on how the ecosystem responds. If merchants absorb the additional cost, there may be little or no visible impact on the consumer. If the cost is reflected in pricing or an additional payment-related charge, consumers may have to pay it as part of the product’s cost.
Whether and to what extent merchants pass such costs on to consumers is yet to be seen.

stories.headline: IND vs WI T20Is: West Indies’ beacon of Hope ready for some redemption
stories.deck: The West Indian’s batting graph has gone north ever since landing in India; after five outings against the Men in Blue across three ODIs and two T20Is, Hope has added 432 golden runs to his international tally
stories.bodyText:
Shai has been a beacon of Hope for Caribbean cricket.
The West Indian’s batting graph has gone north ever since landing in India. After five outings against the Men in Blue across three ODIs and two T20Is, Hope has added 432 golden runs to his international tally.
It’s tough to pick out his best knock from the last two weeks. He has three centuries and a half-century to choose from. Perhaps he will narrow it down to the unbeaten ones: 162 in the New Chandigarh ODI and 102 in the Ranchi T20I. He did hit the winning runs in both, each sealing the Windies’ highest successful run-chase in that particular format (352 and 250, respectively).
What may tip the balance towards his exploits at the JSCA Stadium would be that it was his first T20I century (always special).
“I think people underrate Hope a lot. He is a guy who can block out noise and just focus on what he has to do. Because when everything seems to be going wrong, he’s still up there giving his best and performing for the team,” West Indies all-rounder Roston Chase said after the visitors’ record chase on Friday (October 9, 2026).
Hope is not one to use brute force — a trait popular among the West Indian willow-wielders — and he has often had to face critiques about his strike-rate. That has been taken care of for now with his ball-striking against India (SR of 112.10 in ODIs and 187.80 in T20Is).
“People play down his stats and record in T20 cricket. They always say he either bats too slowly or he bats for himself. I’m always happy when I see him do well. I know he’s an ultimate professional who tries to tick every box and do the right things all the time,” Chase added.
And Hope’s upgrade wasn’t just built on hope. “He’s done a lot of gym work to make himself stronger in terms of hitting the ball over the ropes. He also practises a lot of range hitting to get in those strong positions,” Chase explained.
Hope’s heroics even drew praise from the opposition camp.
“We know Shai is a world-class cricketer. We respect him for what he has done in white-ball cricket,” head coach Gautam Gambhir said after India’s six-wicket loss.
Hope — as the famous Shawshank Redemption dialogue goes — is a good thing, maybe the best of things. Now, Shai Hope’s best is here, ready for some redemption!

stories.headline: How Neeraj Chopra's javelin helped Rohit Yadav win Asian Games bronze
stories.deck: Rohit Yadav made an impressive mark at the Asian Games javelin final with support from Neeraj Chopra, who lent him a javelin after Yadav’s was damaged. With a throw of 84.35m, Yadav clinched a bronze medal. This victory led to a heartfelt message from Chopra, eager to join forces in future competitions. Yadav is now set to refine his skills for upcoming international events.
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: When Rohit Yadav stepped onto the field in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, for the Asian Games javelin final, he carried more than a piece of sporting equipment. In his hand was a signed javelin belonging to Olympic and world champion Neeraj Chopra — a quiet gesture of support that would accompany him to an international podium.
The story began in June, when Yadav struck gold at the National Inter State Senior Athletics Championships in Bhubaneswar with a personal best of 87.05m. Upon returning to his training base in NIS Patiala, he discovered that his preferred javelin had bent, apparently during air transit in its protective PVC tube in the aircraft’s cargo hold.
Yadav subsequently competed at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow with a borrowed implement, finishing seventh with 81.56m in cold, windy conditions. With the Asian Games approaching, he faced the prospect of competing without his trusted javelin.
“For the Asian Games, I didn’t have my own javelin. My preferred one was damaged and had bent. While coming to Delhi from Patiala for the Indian Athletics Final Series on Sept 10, I spoke to Neeraj bhai,” Yadav told TOI.
“We have been in regular touch. I knew he had returned to India for rehabilitation. I told him I didn’t have a javelin of my own for the Asian Games. 
He immediately came to my rescue and sent me one of his signed javelins through a private taxi service to the Jawaharlal Nehru (JLN) stadium,” he added.
Chopra had withdrawn from the remainder of the season, including the Asian Games, to recover from an ankle ligament injury. His absence left India without its two-time defending champion, but his gesture ensured that a fellow Indian thrower had the equipment he needed.
There was, however, a catch. Yadav could not use the javelin in Delhi because it had not been registered with the Technical Information Centre (TIC) for inspection. He borrowed another registered implement for the event, then carefully packed Chopra’s gift for Japan.
“At the Asian Games, I registered two javelins with the TIC. But I used the one Neeraj bhai gave me. I had a good grip and hold over it, and with that javelin I made the winning throw to secure bronze with 84.35m,” he said.
“I will remain thankful to Neeraj bhai. I have kept that javelin with me and will use it in future competitions as well.”
After his competition, Rohit listened to Chopra’s congratulatory voice message.
“He told me to enjoy the win and savour my first big international medal. He said that when he returns fully fit, we will compete together, and that I have a long way to go.”
Back home in Uttar Pradesh’s Jaunpur, Yadav is taking the off-season to spend time with family until Diwali.
“I want to earn a Diamond League entry, compete internationally and qualify for the World Championships next year. The ultimate target remains the Los Angeles Olympics,” he added.

stories.headline: Only second ever! Hope scripts history against India with record-breaking ton
stories.deck: West Indies captain Shai Hope became only the second player after Australia's Shane Watson to score centuries in all three formats against India. Hope smashed an unbeaten 102 off 45 balls, helping West Indies chase 250 to win by six wickets in Ranchi. The victory marked their highest successful T20I chase and levelled the five-match series at 1-1.
stories.bodyText:
West Indies captain 
Shai Hope
 created history on Friday by becoming only the second player in the world to score centuries in all three formats of international cricket against India.
He achieved the milestone with an unbeaten 102 off 45 balls in the second T20I in Ranchi, helping the West Indies chase down a target of 250 and win by six wickets.
Hope's explosive innings guided his team to victory in just 18.3 overs, with four wickets down.
The result also marked the highest successful T20I run chase in West Indies history and the highest successful chase by any team against India in the format.
Shane Watson Shares the Record
Former Australia all-rounder Shane Watson is the only other player to have scored at least one century in Tests, ODIs and T20Is against India. Watson achieved the feat during his international career, scoring one hundred in each format.
Before his latest knock, Hope had already scored one Test century and five ODI centuries against India. His unbeaten hundred in Ranchi completed the set by giving him his first T20I century against the Indian team.
England's Jos Buttler and Australia's Glenn Maxwell have also scored centuries against India in Tests and T20Is, but neither has scored a hundred against India in ODIs.
Hope joins elite T20I list
Hope is the second West Indies batter, after 
Evin Lewis
, to score a T20I century against India. Lewis has scored two hundreds against India in the shortest format, making him one of the few players to achieve the feat more than once.
Hope's latest achievement adds to his growing record against India and highlights his ability to perform across formats. His match-winning innings in Ranchi not only secured a historic personal milestone but also helped West Indies level the five-match T20I series at 1-1.

stories.headline: The World title match is like an hourglass… it’s always the same opponent: Nepomniachtchi
stories.deck: The Russian GM recently got a measure of revenge for his 2021 World championship loss, beating Magnus Carlsen to help his side win the Global Chess League. He talks about the upcoming Gukesh-Sindarov clash, the dynamics of title matches and the next generation
stories.bodyText:
Ian Nepomniachtchi’s victory over Magnus Carlsen of Alpine APL Pipers in the final match of the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League led his team Ganges Grandmasters to an unlikely maiden title in Bengaluru. Back in 2021, he had unsuccessfully challenged Carlsen in the World title match; that would turn out to be the Norwegian’s last defence of his crown. One of the most gifted players of his generation, the Russian shared the World blitz title with Carlsen two years ago. Excerpts from an interview Nepomniachtchi gave The Hindu:
You returned to the Global Chess League after missing out on the last two editions.
I had some visa issues, unfortunately, in 2024, and last year I skipped. Back in 2023, I played in the inaugural edition. I found it interesting. It is really fun for players. Because, sometimes, especially classical chess, it’s a little bit too controlled. And it sometimes can be a bit boring, not only for players, but even for the fans, I believe.
The GCL’s format brings a lot of different imbalances. You don’t know the colour before the game, at least for the first part of the league, as it is decided by the toss, and you have four points for a win with black pieces and three with white. It is all fun and brings in some extra excitement. So, all in all, I think it is a good tournament to have in your calendar.
How did you find the response from the Bengaluru crowd? There were full houses for most days and the fans were cheering. That is not something you usually see at a chess tournament.
Yes. I have played a lot in Dortmund, where you get fans. But normally chess fans there are quite elderly, and sometimes they just start snoring in the first row. So that is a bit funny.
Everyone can hear this, but not arbiters. Jokes aside, I think the audience here is very respectful. I would never hear any sound from them during the games.
You have played for the World championship twice, against Magnus Carlsen and Ding Liren. How do you view this year’s World title match between D. Gukesh and Javokhir Sindarov?
The World championship match is always very special. It is like an hourglass. It is not like the round of the tournament when you can play one game badly and catch up later by beating another guy. It is always the same opponent. If we analyse the results for the past 16 or 17 months, there is some bad news for the Gukesh fans. He has lost roughly 90 Elo points or so.
Yes, he has dropped way down from being the World No. 3.
It is probably a question to him and to his team — What is going on, what is happening? He is just a bit different from what we saw in 2024, especially in Budapest and in Toronto. But, you know, that doesn’t guarantee some easy way to the crown for Javokhir. Because, you know, they are both very young and form can be very volatile sometimes.
Of course, as of now, Sindarov starts as a huge favourite, but I wouldn’t say it is something like 80 to 20. I think it should be more like 65 to 35. And I believe who wins the first game will be important. If Gukesh manages to win one, especially in the beginning, or at least not lose, the match could become unclear, as he will get some confidence. But if Sindarov starts with a win, it could easily turn into a snowball.
Before your own World championship match against Ding Liren, I remember talking to Viswanathan Anand, and he had picked you as the favourite in a close match, but you lost in the tie-breaker. How difficult is it to prepare for and play in a World championship match?
The match is always tough. It is probably not the match itself. Playing itself is the easiest part, because it is what you are used to doing since childhood. But the preparation takes three months or even half a year or so. You basically live a very different life from what you normally do. It is a huge period of time, and you have to be completely focused.
Back then, watching the last round [of the Candidates], I really wanted [Hikaru] Nakamura to qualify. Okay, I really liked Ding so much more as a chess player. But sadly something happened with him. During the match he was shaky at first. But then in the middle of the match he played a sequence of quite decent games. It is very difficult when it goes down the rollercoaster, like, win-lose-win-lose. Even if you have the upper hand, even when you lead on the score, it drains some extra energy from you.
Before that, in the Carlsen match, you had drawn the first five games…
I had worked quite a bit on my chess and physical condition. But I could never predict I wouldn’t sleep at all during the match. So, basically, my brain just fried. And in Game Six, I committed a couple of blunders. And I let him into this very unpleasant ending, which I surely didn’t want to appear. I could have made as many draws as possible, but playing for a win also brings you to some unknown territory sometimes. And whenever it came down to something, even simple calculation... my brain hadn’t rested properly, I started blundering things. It was a big experience, of course, but also he played so well.
Who are the young players you are currently impressed with?
Well, now you just blink once, and some young player already becomes a Grandmaster or reaches 2700.
[Yagiz Kaan] Erdogmus is quite promising indeed. It is hard to compare him to a player like me, because now it is so much easier to learn opening in a perfect way because of computers. Now it is a whole new situation.
I was quite impressed when I played a classical game against [Faustino] Oro. He is 12 years old, and he knew so much about the opening. When I was 12, I knew a couple of lines, here and there. And I had a rating of around 2300 or even 2400. So, I was not completely talentless. But, my opening knowledge was not like this. That is a big difference between players of my generation and this one.
Back home in Russia, we have some hopes about Roman Shogdzhiev. He seems to be promising. And perhaps he could also try to get his GM title, you know, maybe set a new record.
Because of the Ukraine war, Russia cannot play in tournaments like the Olympiad. You were one of those chess players who signed an open letter to Vladimir Putin demanding an end to the military action.
As a citizen, I think it is fine to have your position.

briefs.headline: First time in 149 years: Australia make unique record in first Test vs South Africa
briefs.deck: Australia's 18-member squad has an average age of around 32.6, with only three players under 30.
briefs.bodyText:
Australia fielded the oldest playing XI in their men's Test history in the first Test against South Africa in Durban on Friday, with all 11 players aged 30 or above. It was the first time in 149 years that an Australian men's Test XI did not include a player in his 20s.
Captain 
Pat Cummins
 won the toss and chose to bat, with Australia's playing XI having an average age of 34.59. According to cricket statistician Ric Finlay, as quoted by News18, it was the seventh-oldest Test XI of all time and the oldest in around 100 years.
At 38, spinner Nathan Lyon was the oldest member of the side, while Matt Renshaw, 30, was the youngest. Five players were aged 35 or above: Lyon, Steve Smith (37), Mitchell Starc (36), Alex Carey (35) and Josh Hazlewood (35).
Australia's regular rotation of openers had ensured that the team included at least one player under 30 for months. However, that changed with the recall of Nic Maddinson, 34, for the Durban Test.
Maddinson was playing his first Test since December 2016. He has featured in only three Tests, all of them in that year.
Australia's 18-member squad has an average age of around 32.6, with only three players under 30. Cooper Connolly, 23, is the youngest, followed by Cameron Green, 27, and Sam Harper, 29. 
Green has regularly featured in the playing XI but has struggled for form in recent times.
Meanwhile, South Africa's pace attack, without their spearhead Kagiso Rabada, restricted Australia to 187/6 before bad light and rain brought an early end to the first day of the opening Test at Kingsmead in Durban on Friday.
Despite Rabada's absence, Anrich Nortje, Wiaan Mulder and Marco Jansen made good use of the early movement and bounce on a pitch with a tinge of grass after Australia chose to bat. Mulder struck first by dismissing Travis Head for nine, before Jansen ended Maddinson's scoreless 33-ball stay on his return to Test cricket, leaving Australia at 24/2.
Marnus Labuschagne, who scored 37, and Smith, who made 25, steadied the innings with a 60-run partnership for the third wicket off 94 balls. Smith, who moved past Steve Waugh to become Australia's third-highest run-scorer in men's Tests, hit two sixes off spinner Keshav Maharaj before Jansen dismissed him after lunch.
Australia had won the toss and opted to bat in the first match of the three-Test World Test Championship series.

briefs.headline: IND vs WI second T20: Shai Hope, Sherfane Rutherford dazzle as West Indies draws level
briefs.deck: Shai Hope hits an unbeaten 102 off just 45 deliveries while Sherfane Rutherford smashes a 37-ball 84 as the Men in Maroon pull off their highest chase in the shortest format; Samson’s knock goes in vain
briefs.bodyText:
The Indian juggernaut has finally been halted.
Chasing may be the preferred template in modern T20Is, but not when you have to hunt down 250. That was the tall order in front of the West Indies at the JSCA Stadium on Friday (October 9, 2026).
Conventional wisdom would’ve predicted an easy win for the defending team, but not against a marauding West Indian batting order.
The Men in Maroon made light work of what looked like an insurmountable task, gunning down the target in 18.3 overs and pulling off a stunning six-wicket victory in the second T20I.
After Mayank Yadav’s fiery opening burst (three for 36), Shai Hope (102 n.o., 45b, 6x4, 9x6) and Sherfane Rutherford (84, 37b, 7x4, 7x6) kept up with the asking rate, and then some.
Kuldeep Yadav could have removed Rutherford at the halfway stage had Mayank held on to a regulation catch. The left-arm wrist-spinner got his man when the southpaw was caught behind in the 15th over.
At that point, after the breathtaking 120-run stand off 54 deliveries, West Indies still needed 72 off 35 balls. Hope and Romario Shepherd (34 n.o., 13b, 3x4, 3x6) then went on to seal a memorable win.
The two final sixes that Hope hit off Axar Patel not only brought up his century but also signalled West Indies’ highest successful run chase in T20Is.
Earlier, the Indian willow-wielders sent the visitors on a leather hunt to amass 249 for five, with Sanju Samson (82, 41b, 9x4, 4x6) being the protagonist.
Kamil Pooran dropping a straightforward catch straightaway unshackled Samson, who was batting on six.
After getting smashed off a free-hit right after the lost opportunity, Akeal Hosein bore the brunt of Samson’s brilliant strokeplay.
Though Samson’s trigger movement was almost always to the leg-side, the shots he hit covered the entire ground. Roston Chase — who had earlier dismissed Abhishek Sharma — castled Ishan Kishan (43, 22b, 6x4, 2x6) to break the 97-run stand before removing another left-hander, No. 4 Shivam Dube.
India lost momentum as well as Samson, who holed out to Kamil at third-man off Springer.
Shreyas Iyer (40, 18b, 3x4, 3x6) and Tilak Varma (44 n.o., 18b, 3x4, 3x6), however, built on the foundation.
Tilak was particularly ruthless against Springer after getting a life caught off a no-ball. Springer’s 23-run 20th over took India to 249, which proved nowhere near enough once Hope’s men took strike.

briefs.headline: Hope springs eternal as West Indies pull off highest chase in T20Is in Ranchi
briefs.deck: Hope and Sherfane Rutherford turned the match on its head with a 120-run stand for the fourth wicket. Rutherford smashed 84 off 37 balls, while Hope remained unbeaten on 102 off 45 as the West Indies chased down India's 250-run target with nine balls to spare.
briefs.bodyText:
Skipper 
Shai Hope
 led from the front with a 45-ball 102 as the West Indies pulled off a record chase to beat India by six wickets in the second T20 International and level the five-match series 1-1 in Ranchi on Friday.
The West Indies looked in trouble when Mayank Yadav struck twice in the opening over of their chase and then dismissed Rovman Powell in the sixth over, leaving the visitors at 58/3. But Hope and 
Sherfane Rutherford
 turned the match on its head with a 120-run stand for the fourth wicket. Rutherford smashed 84 off 37 balls, while Hope remained unbeaten on 102 off 45 as the West Indies chased down India's 250-run target with nine balls to spare.
Hope and Rutherford's 120-run partnership was the West Indies' highest for the fourth wicket in T20Is, surpassing the previous record of 103 set by Dwayne Bravo and Shimron Hetmyer.
Hope sealed the historic chase by hitting Axar Patel for a six, bringing up his century in the process. The total also became the West Indies' highest successful chase in T20I cricket.
At the halfway stage, India's total of 249/5 had put them in a strong position, but the West Indies made light work of the target despite losing wickets in the powerplay. 
The visitors hit 20 sixes and 21 fours, scoring 204 runs through boundaries alone.
Earlier, Sanju Samson returned to form with an 82-run knock before Shreyas Iyer and Tilak Varma's quickfire knocks helped India post 249/5 in the first innings.
After four consecutive low scores, Samson struck a 21-ball half-century, his ninth in T20Is, and shared a 97-run stand off 43 balls with Ishan Kishan. Their partnership helped India reach their highest-ever T20I total against the West Indies.
The pair took India to 139/1 in 11 overs at a run rate of more than 12. Kishan contributed 43 off 22 balls, hitting six fours and two sixes.
West Indies off-spinner Roston Chase, however, broke the partnership after returning to the attack during the middle overs, taking two wickets in successive overs.
Kishan and Shivam Dube, who scored seven, were both bowled while attempting shots across the line. India's decision to promote Dube to No. 4 did not work, as he managed only seven runs off 10 balls before being dismissed.
Samson's innings also came to an end in the 15th over, 18 runs short of a century. His ramp shot over deep backward point went straight to Kamil Pooran.
India lost three wickets for 23 runs during the middle overs, but skipper Iyer kept the scoring rate up. Having struck his maiden T20I century in Lucknow, he continued his run with an 18-ball 40, counter-attacking with a series of quick runs.
Tilak, meanwhile, remained unbeaten on 44 off 18 balls to help India finish with 249/5.

briefs.headline: Match-winner on captaincy debut! Farhan leads Pak to stunning chase vs Sri Lanka
briefs.deck: Sahibzada Farhan made a remarkable debut as captain, scoring 89 runs and guiding Pakistan to an impressive win over Sri Lanka, successfully chasing down 183. The aggressive pairing with Maaz Sadaqat shone through, sealing victory with seven balls left in the first T20I. Sri Lanka had set a competitive stage, thanks to Lahiru Udara's 91 runs. The anticipation builds for the upcoming matches…
briefs.bodyText:
Sahibzada Farhan
 celebrated his elevation to 
Pakistan
’s T20I captaincy in spectacular fashion, smashing a blistering 89 to steer his side to a four-wicket victory over Sri Lanka in the opening match of the three-game series in Rawalpindi on Friday.
Chasing 183 for victory, Farhan’s explosive 53-ball knock, combined with Maaz Sadaqat’s maiden T20I half-century, powered Pakistan to 187/6 in 18.5 overs. The hosts secured a 1-0 lead in the series after overcoming a spirited Sri Lankan effort led by opener 
Lahiru Udara
.
Farhan hammered 10 fours and four sixes in a commanding innings, while Sadaqat struck 50 off just 29 deliveries to put Pakistan firmly in control of the chase.
Farhan, Sadaqat turn the chase into a run-fest
Pakistan’s opening pair of Farhan and Fakhar Zaman provided an aggressive start, putting on 54 runs off just 31 balls. Fakhar contributed 21 before departing, but the early momentum continued as Sadaqat joined his captain at the crease.
Sri Lanka’s pace attack struggled to contain the onslaught. Tall fast bowler Dushmantha Chameera conceded 32 runs in his two powerplay overs as Pakistan made a flying start to the chase.
Sadaqat immediately took the attack to Eshan Malinga, striking two sixes and a four in his first four deliveries against the bowler. 
He then combined with Farhan in a blistering 92-run partnership off 53 balls that put Pakistan on course for victory.
Sadaqat reached his maiden T20I half-century in just 28 balls but fell on the very next delivery, trapped leg-before-wicket by Maheesh Theekshana, who finished with 2/36.
Sri Lanka briefly fought back as Chameera claimed his 100th T20 wicket by having Hasan Nawaz caught behind down the leg side. Theekshana then bowled Saim Ayub for eight with a delivery that stayed low.
Farhan, however, continued to counterattack, taking on Theekshana with a six and three fours in one over. His brilliant innings finally ended when Sahan Arachchige pulled off a spectacular diving catch at midwicket, but Pakistan needed only three more runs to win at that stage.
Udara’s 91 lifts Sri Lanka to competitive total
Earlier, Udara struck a superb 91 off 55 balls to help Sri Lanka post 182/8 against a revamped Pakistan pace attack featuring debutants Mohammad Imran and Razaullah.
Naseem Shah, recalled to the T20I squad after Shaheen Afridi and Mohammad Haris were left out, made an immediate impact by dismissing Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis for one in the opening over. Imran also impressed on debut, claiming 2/21, while Naseem finished with 3/36.
Sri Lanka struggled early before Udara steadied the innings. He added 60 runs with Kamindu Mendis, who scored 23, and followed it with a 57-run stand alongside Dasun Shanaka, who made 18.
Udara reached his half-century off 32 balls and struck 11 fours and a six before falling in Naseem’s final over. Sri Lanka scored 66 runs in the final six overs to give their bowlers a challenging target, but Farhan’s captaincy debut proved memorable as Pakistan completed the chase with seven balls to spare.
Rawalpindi will host the remaining two matches on Sunday and next Tuesday.

briefs.headline: APL: Chiefs, Yodhas post wins; Royals stumble
briefs.bodyText:
Chola Chiefs defeated Kakatiya Knights 6-2 to register its first win of Archery Premier League season-2 at the People’s Plaza here on Friday. Colombia’s Alejandra Usquiano, on her APL debut, shot all eight arrows for 10s, with the Chiefs’ tactical tweak paying off against Nico Wiener’s Knights.
Chiefs’ tactic of having their compound archers Rishabh Yadav and Usquiano shoot both their arrows in the first half helped start the contest with a perfect half of 40. Knights, in the end, couldn’t recover from the scoreboard pressure.
While the compound archers were on fire, Chiefs’ recurve stars Deepika Kumari and Marcus D’Almeida also joined the party to help it clinch the final set 79-76 and the match.
In the second match, Chero Archers got the better of Rajputana Royals. Royals took the first set but couldn’t sustain the momentum. Archers’ move to substitute in Atanu Das for Yashdeep Bhoge ahead of the second set, proved to be a masterstroke as he and Casey Kaufhold helped the team come from behind to win 6-2.
Later, Prithviraj Yodhas registered its first win, beating Mighty Marathas 6-2. Like Royals before them, Marathas began well but couldn’t build on it.
Abhishek Verma-led Yodhas were a whisker away from a perfect 80 in the third set, before the eighth arrow from Matias Grande slipped into the nine zone. But they had done enough by then to get a leg up on Marathas.

briefs.headline: Comeback man Hoblidhar storms to win in 100m
briefs.bodyText:
Last year, Manikanta Hoblidhar became the first Indian man to go under 10.20 seconds in the 100m, setting a new national record and throwing down the gauntlet for the rest of the sprinters.
Cut to March this year and the Karnataka man, hoping to add international success to his growing list of achievements on the domestic circuit, broke down. A Grade-2 hamstring tear during the National relay championships led to the revelation of a blood clot in his tendons as well, throwing his entire year into disarray. He missed the Commonwealth and Asian Games and the World Relays but most importantly, he was left far behind on the track.
On Friday, the 24-year-old took the first steps back to national reckoning, clocking 10.25 seconds to win the 65th National Open Athletics Championships at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium here.
“I had targeted better timing here but an upset stomach since last night didn’t help. I also slowed towards the end because after such a long break, you are a little cautious. My biggest regret, however, is that my injury also affected the relay team and India’s chances of a medal. But now the body is fine and my aim is to clock 10.00 in the coming season,” Hoblidhar said, adding that there was still work to be done before gaining optimum fitness ahead of the next season. Lalu Prasad Bhoi was second in 10.43s and Lukik Melge 3rd (10.45s).
In the women’s section, Aichi-Nagoya bronze medalist and national record holder Manpreet Kaur was the only shot-putter to cross the 17m mark, taking the top spot with a best throw of 17.07m. The 21-year-old Anjli, in her first national level event, stunned the field including favourite Priya Mohan to clock a personal best of 53.37s in the 400m.
Moumita Mandal, also returning from an injury layoff, topped the heat before taking the 100m hurdles in 13.48 seconds. However, Servin Sebastian, leading all the way, was pushed to fourth spot in the racewalk half-marathon in the morning session after being adjudged of technical violation and penalised two minutes for loss of contact.

briefs.headline: India’s top-tier league set for a new chapter
briefs.bodyText:
The Indian Super League begins a new chapter on Saturday, with clubs taking charge of the ISL’s commercial future and the competition returning to a full-fledged home-and-away format.
The shift marks a departure from the ISL’s previous structure. While the All India Football Federation will retain administrative control and oversee key operational aspects, the clubs will hold the commercial rights, giving them a greater stake in shaping the league’s future.
The change brings both opportunity and responsibility. The clubs’ ability to generate revenue and create a compelling match-day experience will have a direct bearing on their financial health.
However, the build-up has been marked by uncertainty, as was the case last year. The announcement of the fixture list was delayed, as was the signing of a new broadcast deal. Jamshedpur FC, owned by Tata Steel, and Diamond Harbour FC both withdrew.
For the 13 clubs that remain, success — both financial and sporting — will depend on what happens on the pitch. Entertaining football and competitive contests will be crucial to attracting new followers and retaining existing ones.
The return to a double round-robin format should help. After a curtailed, single-leg campaign last time, the teams will face each other home and away, restoring the rhythm of a conventional league season. The longer schedule will test squad depth, fitness and consistency while giving coaches more scope for tactical adjustments.
The supporters, meanwhile, will play a crucial role in determining whether the reset succeeds. Despite the uncertainty that surrounded Indian football last season, strong local following helped clubs such as Mohun Bagan Super Giant, East Bengal FC and Bengaluru FC keep interest in the stands.
As the season unfolds, all stakeholders will hope that a sustainable model takes shape. Saturday’s double-header marks the beginning of that test and another attempt by the ISL to establish a stable footing.

briefs.headline: Pageant or pillar: what exactly is the Laver Cup?
briefs.deck: Where does the tournament, modelled on golf’s Ryder Cup, stand in tennis? What does it bring to the sport? And for how long will its carefully engineered success endure?
briefs.bodyText:
Rod Laver in tennis is like Don Bradman in cricket. The famed left-hander is the only player to have achieved the Grand Slam — the herculean feat of winning all four Majors in a single year — twice. It’s like Bradman’s astronomical average of 99.94, a measure of greatness unlikely to be emulated or surpassed in a million years.
In 2017, when the inaugural Laver Cup was held in Prague, it seemed like the perfect honour for the legendary Aussie. Modelled on golf’s Ryder Cup, the biennial competition with a 100-year history that pits Europe against the United States of America, the Laver Cup broadened the scope — in line with tennis’ global footprint — to bring Europe face to face with the World.
Federer’s brainchild
That the tournament was the brainchild of Roger Federer, the winner of 20 Slam titles, gave it enormous legitimacy. The elegant Swiss has often been spoken of as the ‘GOAT’ (Greatest of All Time), and for him to celebrate and immortalise Laver was the ultimate acknowledgement of who stood at the sport’s zenith.
Nine years since that festive September weekend, where does the Laver Cup stand and what does it bring to tennis? Has the association with two of tennis’ greatest champions helped it acquire an exalted status?
At the outset, it has all the ingredients that make any modern-day sporting extravaganza tick — participation from the elite (the three highest-ranked players from each region are automatic picks); eye-popping prize money (appearance fee and a $250,000 bonanza for each of the six players in the winning team); a weekend window without competing big-ticket competitions in a calendar that is bursting at the seams.
For the first seven editions, Europe and World were captained by icons Bjorn Borg and John McEnroe, and saw wholesome participation from Federer, Rafael Nadal, Novak Djokovic and Andy Murray, who collectively won an astonishing 69 Majors from 2003 to 2023. Since then, the captaincy has moved on to Yannick Noah and Andre Agassi, and the cream of the present era, led by the irresistible Carlos Alcaraz, has embraced it too.
If the signature black tennis court makes the Laver Cup a tournament apart, the concert-like setting with dark-arena lighting imparts a posh, cinematic look. It showcases both singles and doubles, and has adopted a format that ensures that the tie is alive on all three days.
It helps that tennis, one of the foremost individual sports, has incrementally warmed to team events, ensuring that the idea of the collective isn’t limited to just the more-than-a-century-old Davis Cup.
The sense of camaraderie championships like the United Cup — the season-opening joint-venture between ATP, WTA and Tennis Australia — and the Laver Cup evoke, and the tactical back and forth between a star-studded bench and players on court, have made for great viewing.
“I never cared more than winning this one,” proclaimed World No. 22 Alexander Bublik, who played the 2026 Laver Cup in London two weeks ago. “I never cared as much in a quarterfinal of a Slam than the doubles that I played [here].”
That Federer brought the curtains down on his storied career at a Laver Cup doubles fixture in 2022 alongside Nadal says it all. Federer and Nadal faced each other 40 times in one of tennis’ greatest rivalries. But little would anyone have imagined that their final act would be one of brotherhood, sitting side by side, holding each other’s hands, and sobbing uncontrollably.
Part organic, part pretentious
Yet, for all the grandeur and the theatre, there is an unmistakable feeling that the Laver Cup is straddling the division between a tennis exhibition and a hard-nosed competition. Part of the bonhomie appears organic, but it is also pretentious.
Davis Cup, tennis’ premier team championship, is replete with tales of polar opposites featuring in the team for a common cause. The most high-profile example is of the United States team that reached the final in 1984 under the captaincy of Arthur Ashe wherein McEnroe and Jimmy Connors went the whole campaign without speaking to each other.
In contrast, the Laver Cup looks like a pageant. “Players talk in a more friendly way,” Casper Ruud told The Athletic in 2024. “You can actually get to know your competitors. Daniil [Medvedev] is a father and we can talk about his family and how it is to be a father. Sometimes I forget that we are normal people as well.”
There are contradictions galore. The Laver Cup and men’s professional tennis’ governing body ATP have been partners since 2019, even allowing matches at the event to be counted in players’ head-to-head records. But without any ranking points, the Laver Cup is also uncoupled from the pulls and pressures of the rest of the Tour.
The grant of official status is in itself debatable, for matches in the Laver Cup aren’t full-fledged contests, with the third set just a 10-point tie-breaker. The scoring system — one point for a win on Friday, two on Saturday, and three on Sunday, with 13 required to lift the trophy — is a masterclass in manufacturing stakes.
When Federer was still an active member of the Tour, there persisted an awkward situation where a player expected to be treated on par with the others by the ATP had a business relationship with that very body. Tennis Australia, which conducts the Australian Open, was one of the original investors in the Laver Cup, another potential conflict of interest involving Federer.
There is no question that the Laver Cup is of the stars, by the stars and for the stars. Will this continue as the tennis world transitions from the era of Federer, Nadal and Djokovic to that of Alcaraz, Jannik Sinner and Alexander Zverev?
Alcaraz is no doubt a big draw, as seen in the way he has electrified the setting in the past three editions. But Sinner hasn’t befriended the tournament yet, and but for Zverev’s ascent this year, the tennis universe outside of Alcaraz and Sinner has seemed hollow.
It is also a question of sporting purity. The Ryder Cup famously doesn’t award prize money, and still Rory McIlroy, the six-time Major winner, once proudly said that he would “personally pay for the privilege to play”.
“We’ll never get rid of that gap [with the Ryder Cup],” Tony Godsick, Federer’s long-standing agent who co-founded the Laver Cup, told The Athletic in 2024. “We invest in the brand for the players, for the sponsors, for the fans, for the media.”
Survival of the fittest
The Laver Cup’s aspirational zeal has taken root at a time when tennis governance is splintered. With all four Grand Slams, and governing bodies in ATP, WTA and World Tennis (erstwhile International Tennis Federation), each having a product to shoehorn into a finite calendar, it is about the survival of the fittest.
“There could be too many other tennis events, but this one is working,” insisted Godsick. “We have sold-out crowds, the biggest captains, the best sponsors. Every player loves to play. So the question is: Is there too much Laver Cup? No. I think there is not enough Laver Cup.”
Laver was — and is — a man of quiet confidence. The Laver Cup is evidently not. Success has been carefully engineered. But for how long?
